title: Constrained-burst adapter: per-tenant budget windows and GPU-class preference matrix
creator: Asha Kapoor
description:
Problem: Tenants experience unpredictable cost spikes during short traffic microbursts, which causes either overspend or heavy throttling when using spot/cheap GPUs. Existing budget-gating policies are coarse-grained (daily or per-minute) and do not reflect short-term burst tolerance or GPU-class suitability for particular models. Goals: 1) Introduce a per-tenant constrained-burst adapter that enforces soft budget windows (short-duration spend caps) in addition to existing longer-term budget controls. 2) Add a GPU-class preference matrix that scores GPU classes (e.g., A100x4, H100-80GB, T4) per model-family/tenant to guide routing when falling back off preferred SKUs or spot instances. 3) When soft caps hit, gracefully degrade using an ordered set of mitigations: lightweight quantized variant, lower sequence-length config, or lower-priority background queue. Requirements: - Maintain latency SLOs for interactive tenants where possible. - Avoid triangle of denial (throttle -> shift traffic -> throttle other region) by coordinating burst allowances globally. - Expose per-tenant config in Console and runtime-config API for ops teams. Proposed design: - Short window budget: sliding window (default 1 minute, configurable) in addition to existing daily/rolling budgets. Each request charges against both windows. The short window uses token-bucket semantics with a spend budget (USD or abstract cost units) and a burst reserve. - GPU-class preference matrix: data model maps tenant -> model-family -> ordered list of GPU classes with numeric preference scores and fallback weight multipliers. Example: {"t5-family": [{"gpu":"T4","score":0.2},{"gpu":"A10G","score":0.5},{"gpu":"H100","score":1.0}]} - Routing decision: rank candidate allocations by a combined score: availability_penalty + cost_penalty * cost_weight + gpu_pref_boost. The constrained-burst adapter injects a soft_penalty when short-window budget usage > threshold, which biases routing toward cheaper SKUs or compaction strategies. - Graceful mitigations order: 1) route to cheaper compatible GPU (respecting gpu_pref matrix) 2) select quantized/model-variant with retrain-free pipeline 3) opt into micro-batching with slightly higher tail latency 4) enqueue to best-effort slot. - Visibility: Console surfaces short-window budget burn rate, projected 1-min spend, and active mitigations per tenant. Implementation notes: - Short-window budget maintained in memory with periodic persistence to durable store for audit. Use approximate counters and leaky-bucket to keep overhead low. - GPU preference matrix stored in config service (gRPC) with hot-reload TTL. - Router changes limited to a pluggable cost scorer so we can A/B test scoring weights. - Backpressure: when global headroom low, adapter emits 'soft-fence' state that reduces burst allowance uniformly across tenants (fairshare). API/Config examples (pseudo YAML string): """
tenant_config:
  short_window:
    window_seconds: 60
    budget_units: 20.0
    burst_reserve: 5.0
  gpu_pref:
    t5-family:
      - gpu: H100
        score: 1.0
      - gpu: A10G
        score: 0.6
      - gpu: T4
        score: 0.2
router:
  cost_weight: 0.7
  availability_weight: 0.2
  gpu_pref_boost: 0.1
"""
Metrics and success criteria: - Reduction in minute-level spend spikes by 60% for customers in the rollout cohort. - No more than 5% increase in p95 latency for interactive requests across affected tenants (target for mitigations 2-3). - Dashboard shows actionable signals: short_window_burn_rate, mitigations_applied_count, fallback_gpu_ratio. Rollout plan: 1) Implement adapter and scorer behind feature flag (runtime) 2) Canary on internal tenants + 3 low-risk customers (2 weeks) 3) Expand to 25% of tenants with opt-out config 4) Full rollout and documentation. Danger/Risks: - Mis-scoring may route traffic to GPUs that produce severe latency regressions for certain models. Mitigation: restrict GPU swaps to only those marked compatible in the model catalog and require per-model latency estimates. - Accounting drift between short-window and billing could confuse customers. Mitigation: surface both abstract cost units and estimated USD with clear rounding semantics. - Fairness: naive per-tenant burst windows could advantage noisy neighbors. Mitigation: global soft-fence with proportional reduction. Open questions: 1) Do we expose short-window budgets in self-serve Console or keep ops-only for first rollout? 2) How to translate token-level cost to short-window budget units for multi-model workloads? 3) What is the default acceptable burst_reserve (5 units is a placeholder)?
